newsitem.title: USA: US economic growth rate key to price outlook - Parry.
newsitem.headline: US economic growth rate key to price outlook - Parry.

text.p: The pace at which the U.S. economy grows compared to its underlying trend rate will be a key factor in determining whether the risks of a pickup in inflation will increase, the head of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said Wednesday.

"In my view, the trend rate of growth is about 2 percent. I would use that as a benchmark as to what happens to growth," San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry said in response to a question following a speech to the National Association Business of Economists. "If it's significantly faster than that, I think you'd be concerned," he said.

Parry was answering a question about what the Fed would look at in determining whether to alter its monetary policy stance. Faster-than-trend growth would amplify concerns about strains on resources in the economy, such as tight labor markets, Parry said.

However, the San Francisco Fed chief indicated he would be reassured if the economy were to expand in line with the trend rate. "If the economy grows as I'm anticipating -- that is roughly around trend -- I don't think one has to be particularly concerned about an acceleration of inflation," he said.
On the question of whether the Fed should wait for actual inflation problems to develop before acting, Parry said he hoped the central bank would not pursue that course.
He noted that the effects of interest-rate changes on the economy show up with long lags, and said he would not want to see the Fed fall behind the curve.

"A lot of the studies suggest that for a change in policy to have a perceptible effect on inflation takes a long time, up to two years," Parry said. "So it would seem to me if one waits until one sees a problem, then I'm afraid that you're really behind the eight ball quite a bit."
He added, "I would hope that we can get an earlier indication if problems develop than would be provided by what actually happens to price behavior."

Parry, who is a voting member of the interest-rate setting Federal Open Market Committee this year, spoke at length about the inflation outlook in the speech on Wednesday as well as during an address on Tuesday.
He said the forecast for prices was uncertain but warned of a risk of a pickup in inflation should labor markets remain tight.
Nonetheless, he stressed that any acceleration in inflation would be modest.
Parry described the present state of the jobs market as "on average, tight," saying: "Most people would agree that the labor market is not one where there is a lot of slack at the present time."
In terms of the recent performance of inflation, Parry cited the dollar's strength as one of the factors that has helped to contain price pressures.

Speaking to reporters after his speech, Parry said that the upcoming reports on fourth-quarter U.S. Gross Domestic Product and the Employment Cost Index (ECI) would be important to the Fed's thinking. "I'd say those two statistics are going to get a lot of attention by the markets and certainly by the Fed as well," he said.
The Commerce Department's first estimate of fourth-quarter GDP is due out on January 31. The ECI, produced by the Labor Department, is scheduled for release on January 28.
Asked about a report Wednesday showing a 12.2 percent plunge in housing starts in December, Parry said he still saw prospects for the housing sector as "quite good."

"I think we've had a good run here with regard to housing," he said. "And it seems to me that in the kind of environment that I'm expecting for 1997, I don't think there (would) be any reason to be particularly concerned about prospects for housing."
On the subject of energy prices, Parry said he was not expecting major changes.
Finally, he was also asked to comment on Wednesday's Beige Book report on economic conditions across the country, which said growth has been moderate and described price pressures as moderate.
"It certainly, I think, is consistent," he said. "It basically said that wage pressures were really quite moderate. And I think in general that's true."
